title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol

hero.subtitle: The current standard for Internet email delivery, defining how billions of messages are routed and delivered every day.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5321 is the current definitive specification for SMTP, superseding RFC 2821 (which had itself replaced the original RFC 821). It describes the protocol for reliable and efficient email transfer.

This RFC includes the Extended SMTP (ESMTP) framework, which adds service extension negotiation via the EHLO command. Individual extensions such as STARTTLS, authentication, and pipelining are defined in separate RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 5321 is the current definitive specification of SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), which transfers email reliably and efficiently. It replaces RFC 2821 and includes the ESMTP framework, which lets servers negotiate extensions with the EHLO command.

sections.title: Mail System Architecture
sections.content:
The SMTP mail system consists of several components:

MUAMail User Agent - the email client (Outlook, Thunderbird, Gmail)
MSAMail Submission Agent - accepts mail from MUAs (port 587)
MTAMail Transfer Agent - relays mail between servers (port 25)
MDAMail Delivery Agent - delivers mail to recipient mailboxes
MX RecordDNS record pointing to the receiving mail server for a domain
sections.plainLanguage: Email passes through several components. The mail user agent (MUA) is the email client. The mail submission agent (MSA) accepts mail from clients on port 587. The mail transfer agent (MTA) relays mail between servers on port 25. The mail delivery agent (MDA) places it in the recipient's mailbox.

sections.title: SMTP Extensions
sections.content:
ESMTP allows servers to advertise supported extensions in response to the EHLO command:

EHLO Capability Advertisement
S: 250-mail.example.com Hello
S: 250-SIZE 35882577
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250-STARTTLS
S: 250-AUTH LOGIN PLAIN
S: 250-PIPELINING
S: 250 SMTPUTF8
sections.plainLanguage: When a client greets a server with EHLO, the server replies with a list of the extensions it supports. Examples are SIZE (maximum message size), 8BITMIME, STARTTLS (upgrade to encryption), AUTH, PIPELINING and SMTPUTF8. The client then uses only what the server offers.

sections.title: Mail Delivery Process
sections.content:
1. DNS Lookup
Sending MTA queries DNS for the MX records of the recipient's domain
2. Connection
Connect to the highest-priority MX host on port 25
3. EHLO Exchange
Negotiate capabilities, optionally upgrade to TLS
4. Envelope
Send MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands
5. Message Transfer
Send headers and body via DATA command, terminated by CRLF.CRLF
sections.plainLanguage: The sending server looks up the recipient domain's MX records in DNS and connects to the highest-priority host on port 25. It exchanges EHLO, may upgrade to TLS, then sends MAIL FROM and RCPT TO. Finally it sends the headers and body with DATA, ending with a line holding only a period.

references.text: Klensin, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 5321, October 2008.
Resnick, P., "Internet Message Format", RFC 5322, October 2008.

summary: SMTP is the protocol mail servers use to relay messages. A client opens a TCP connection, introduces itself with EHLO, names the sender and each recipient, sends the message with DATA, and the server answers every command with a numeric reply. RFC 5321 obsoletes RFC 2821 and includes the extension mechanism.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP is the protocol mail servers use to relay email. A client opens a TCP connection, introduces itself with EHLO, names the sender and each recipient, and sends the message with DATA. The server answers every command with a numeric reply. RFC 5321 replaces RFC 2821 and includes the extension mechanism.

tldr.problem: Mail has to move between servers run by different organizations, reliably and in a common way.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection and sends text commands (EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA); the server replies to each with a three-digit code.
tldr.outcome: It remains the standard way email is relayed, extended with options such as STARTTLS and authentication.

today: SMTP is still how email moves between providers. Submission from mail clients typically uses a separate service, with sessions upgraded to TLS using STARTTLS (RFC 3207) or run over implicit TLS. Message content itself follows the Internet Message Format (RFC 5322).
